questions.scenario: A company wants to add medical terminology understanding to their foundation model. They are comparing pre-training a model from scratch on medical literature, fine-tuning an existing FM with labeled clinical examples, and using in-context learning with example medical Q&A pairs in prompts.
questions.stem: How do these approaches rank from MOST to LEAST expensive in compute resources?

options.text: Fine-tuning > Pre-training > In-context learning
In-context learning > Fine-tuning > Pre-training
Pre-training > Fine-tuning > In-context learning
All three approaches have equivalent compute costs

explanation.correct: Pre-training from scratch requires millions of GPU hours on massive datasets (most expensive). Fine-tuning updates existing weights with smaller datasets (moderate cost). In-context learning requires zero training compute — it works entirely within the prompt at inference time.

distractors.A: Fine-tuning is less expensive than pre-training because it starts from an already-trained model and uses smaller datasets.
distractors.B: In-context learning has zero training cost. It is the least expensive approach, not the most expensive.
distractors.D: These approaches differ dramatically in cost — from millions of dollars (pre-training) to zero training cost (in-context learning).

questions.scenario: A startup has a working foundation model but needs it to follow their specific output format (JSON with particular fields) and maintain a formal tone. They have no budget for GPU training compute.
questions.stem: Which customization approach is feasible given their constraint?

options.text: Continued pre-training on format-specific documents
Fine-tuning with labeled examples in the target format
In-context learning — providing format examples and tone instructions directly in the prompt
Training a reward model to align outputs with the desired format

explanation.correct: In-context learning works entirely within the prompt at inference time without modifying model weights. It requires no training compute — the model is guided by instructions and examples provided in the context window.

distractors.A: Continued pre-training requires significant GPU compute to extend training on additional data. This violates the zero-budget constraint.
distractors.B: Fine-tuning updates model weights, requiring GPU compute for the training process. This exceeds the available budget.
distractors.D: Training a reward model requires compute for both the reward model and the RLHF training loop. This is more expensive than fine-tuning.

questions.scenario: A team evaluates a 7B, 13B, and 70B parameter version of the same model family for zero-shot text classification. Without any examples or fine-tuning, the 70B version achieves 89% accuracy, the 13B achieves 74%, and the 7B achieves 58%.
questions.stem: What scaling property does this demonstrate?

options.text: Larger models are more likely to perform tasks well without additional in-context learning or further training
Smaller models are better at zero-shot tasks because they are more focused
Model performance is random and unrelated to parameter count
The accuracy difference is caused by different training data, not model size

explanation.correct: Research demonstrates that larger models of any architecture are more capable — the larger the model, the more likely it works without additional in-context learning or further training. This is consistent with observed scaling laws.

distractors.B: The data shows the opposite — the smallest model has the lowest zero-shot accuracy. Larger models generalize better without examples.
distractors.C: The results show a clear trend (58% → 74% → 89%) correlated with size. This is not random but follows established scaling laws.
distractors.D: The scenario states these are versions of the same model family, implying similar training data. Size is the variable.

questions.scenario: An analytics platform needs to process entire quarterly earnings transcripts (typically 15,000-20,000 tokens) and generate detailed reports (5,000-8,000 tokens). They're evaluating models with context windows of 4K, 32K, and 128K tokens.
questions.stem: Which model is the MINIMUM viable option for this use case?

options.text: The 4K context model — it can process the transcript in chunks
The 32K context model — it can accommodate the input and output within a single context window
The 128K context model — only the largest model can handle text of any length
Any model works because output generation does not consume context window space

explanation.correct: The context window must accommodate both input (up to 20K tokens) and output (up to 8K tokens) = 28K total. The 32K model is the minimum viable option. The 4K model cannot fit the input; the 128K model works but exceeds minimum requirements.

distractors.A: Processing in chunks loses cross-section context needed for coherent report generation. The input (15-20K tokens) alone exceeds the 4K window.
distractors.C: The 128K model works but is not the minimum viable option. The 32K model can accommodate both input and output within constraints.
distractors.D: Both input and output tokens consume context window space. The total must fit within the model's limit.

questions.scenario: A team of three developers is building a generative AI prototype. They need vector search for their RAG pipeline but have no DevOps engineer to manage database clusters, handle patching, or configure auto-scaling.
questions.stem: Which AWS service addresses their operational constraint?

options.text: Self-managed OpenSearch cluster on EC2 with custom scaling scripts
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector requiring manual maintenance windows
Amazon ElastiCache with custom vector indexing code
The vector engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless — providing vector storage and search without infrastructure management

explanation.correct: The vector engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides vector storage and search capabilities without managing vector database infrastructure — no cluster management, patching, or scaling configuration required.

distractors.A: Self-managed OpenSearch on EC2 requires significant DevOps effort for cluster management, scaling, and patching — exactly what the team lacks.
distractors.B: RDS PostgreSQL still requires managing maintenance windows, instance sizing, and patches, even if less than self-managed options.
distractors.C: Custom vector indexing on ElastiCache requires building and maintaining search logic, which demands engineering effort the team doesn't have.

questions.scenario: An enterprise architect is presenting customization options to the board. They need to explain when each approach is appropriate.
questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe when to use specific customization approaches? (Select TWO)

options.text: Use RAG when domain knowledge changes frequently and you need current information without retraining the model
Use fine-tuning when the model needs to adopt a specific behavior pattern or output style that cannot be achieved through prompting alone
Use pre-training from scratch whenever you need any customization — it is always the best approach
Use in-context learning only when you have a budget exceeding $100,000 for training compute
Use RAG only when the model has been pre-trained for fewer than 1 billion tokens

explanation.correct: RAG is ideal for frequently changing information since it retrieves at inference time without retraining. Fine-tuning is appropriate when behavioral patterns or output styles cannot be achieved through prompting alone — it permanently modifies model behavior.

distractors.C: Pre-training from scratch is the most expensive and rarely necessary. Most customization needs are met by fine-tuning, RAG, or in-context learning.
distractors.D: In-context learning has zero training cost — it's the budget-friendly option, not one requiring large budgets.
distractors.E: RAG's applicability depends on knowledge freshness needs and data access requirements, not the model's pre-training token count.

questions.stem: Which AWS database services support vector embedding storage and similarity search for AI applications? (Select THREE)

options.text: Amazon Neptune — graph database with vector search capabilities
Amazon DocumentDB — MongoDB-compatible with vector support
Amazon MemoryDB for Redis — in-memory database with vector indexing
Amazon DynamoDB — key-value store with native vector search
Amazon Timestream — time series database with embedding storage
Amazon QLDB — ledger database with vector verification

explanation.correct: Neptune, DocumentDB, and Redis/MemoryDB all support vector storage for AI applications. Additional options include OpenSearch, Aurora, and RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector.

distractors.D: DynamoDB is optimized for key-value and document access patterns. It does not provide native vector similarity search.
distractors.E: Timestream is designed for time-series data with temporal queries. It does not support vector embedding storage or similarity search.
distractors.F: QLDB is an immutable ledger for transaction verification. It does not provide vector search capabilities.

questions.scenario: A solutions architect is planning their Amazon Bedrock deployment. They need to understand which model configurations support inference through the Bedrock API.
questions.stem: Which model types can you run inference against in Amazon Bedrock? (Select THREE)

options.text: Base foundation models available in the Bedrock model catalog
Custom models created through Bedrock fine-tuning
Models deployed with provisioned throughput for consistent performance
Models self-hosted on EC2 instances in the same VPC
Open-source models downloaded to local SageMaker notebooks
Third-party models accessible only via their own external APIs

explanation.correct: Bedrock supports inference on base foundation models (from the catalog), custom models (fine-tuned within Bedrock), and provisioned throughput models (dedicated capacity). You can test responses with different prompts and parameters across all three.

distractors.D: EC2-hosted models are accessed through their own endpoints, not the Bedrock inference API. Bedrock manages its own model hosting.
distractors.E: SageMaker notebook models are served through SageMaker endpoints, not Bedrock's API.
distractors.F: External third-party APIs are independent services. Bedrock provides access to its own catalog of partner models.

questions.scenario: A production ML team notices their Bedrock-powered chatbot's response quality has degraded over time as user query patterns have shifted. They originally tuned parameters for formal business queries, but users now send more casual, creative requests.
questions.stem: What does this indicate about inference parameter management? (Select TWO)

options.text: Parameters should be continuously monitored and adjusted as usage patterns and requirements evolve
Finding optimal parameters requires experimentation to balance diversity, coherence, and resource efficiency
Parameters set at initial deployment should never be modified in production
Parameter degradation means the model must be retrained from scratch
Only the response length parameter needs adjustment when query patterns change

explanation.correct: Inference parameters require ongoing monitoring and adjustment as requirements evolve. Finding optimal settings is experimental — balancing diversity (for creative queries), coherence (for factual ones), and resource efficiency.

distractors.C: Static parameters cannot adapt to changing usage patterns. The scenario demonstrates exactly why ongoing adjustment is necessary.
distractors.D: Shifting query patterns don't require retraining. Inference parameter adjustment can adapt the model's response behavior without modification.
distractors.E: Multiple parameters interact — temperature, Top P, and Top K all affect how the model handles casual vs formal queries. Adjusting one alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: Beyond accuracy metrics, which operational factors should influence pre-trained model selection for production deployment? (Select THREE)

options.text: Hardware constraints — whether deployment infrastructure can support the model's compute and memory requirements
Maintenance cadence — how frequently the model is updated and whether known issues are addressed
Data privacy implications — whether using the model exposes sensitive data or violates regulations
The model's position on trending leaderboards this week
The model creator's social media presence and follower count
Whether the model's documentation uses dark mode

explanation.correct: Hardware constraints determine deployability, maintenance cadence indicates reliability and support, and data privacy implications determine regulatory compliance. All are critical production considerations beyond raw accuracy.

distractors.D: Leaderboard position fluctuates and may not reflect suitability for your specific production use case and constraints.
distractors.E: Social media presence has no correlation with model quality, reliability, or fitness for production workloads.
distractors.F: Documentation styling is cosmetic and irrelevant to model capabilities or production readiness.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company's product catalog changes weekly with new items, discontinued products, and price updates. They need their AI assistant to always have current product information when answering customer questions.
questions.stem: Why is RAG more appropriate than fine-tuning for this requirement?

options.text: RAG retrieves current data at inference time from an updatable knowledge base, while fine-tuning would require retraining weekly to incorporate catalog changes
RAG is always more accurate than fine-tuning for any use case
Fine-tuning cannot be performed on foundation models
RAG requires less data than fine-tuning to achieve the same level of accuracy

explanation.correct: RAG retrieves from an external knowledge base at inference time. When the catalog updates, only the knowledge base needs updating — no model retraining required. Fine-tuning bakes information into weights, requiring expensive retraining for each update.

distractors.B: RAG and fine-tuning serve different purposes. Fine-tuning is better for behavioral changes; RAG is better for dynamic knowledge. Neither is universally superior.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning is well-supported for foundation models. It's just inappropriate here because the data changes too frequently.
distractors.D: The comparison isn't about data quantity. It's about the operational overhead of weekly retraining vs simply updating a knowledge base.

questions.scenario: A team deploys a 7B parameter model for customer email classification. It achieves acceptable accuracy with few-shot examples in the prompt. Their manager asks why they didn't use the 70B version that performs better in benchmarks.
questions.stem: What is a valid justification for choosing the smaller model when it meets requirements?

options.text: Smaller models always produce higher-quality outputs than larger models
The 7B model meets accuracy requirements at significantly lower inference cost — the 70B model's superior capability is unnecessary overhead for this task
Larger models cannot perform classification tasks
The 7B model has a larger context window than the 70B model

explanation.correct: While larger models are more capable, if the smaller model meets requirements with few-shot prompting, selecting the larger model adds unnecessary cost. The right model balances capability against resource constraints for the specific task.

distractors.A: Larger models generally produce higher-quality outputs. The justification is cost-efficiency when requirements are already met, not quality superiority.
distractors.C: Larger models can perform classification tasks — typically better. The point is that the smaller model already meets the requirement.
distractors.D: Context window size is an architectural choice, not inherently tied to parameter count. This is not a valid justification.

questions.scenario: A research team builds a literature review tool that must ingest 10 research papers simultaneously (averaging 8,000 tokens each) and generate a synthesis comparing their findings (approximately 3,000 tokens).
questions.stem: What is the minimum context window required for this use case?

options.text: 8,000 tokens — the size of the longest individual paper
16,000 tokens — double the average paper length for safety margin
80,000 tokens — only the input matters since output is generated separately
83,000 tokens — total input (10 × 8,000) plus output (3,000)

explanation.correct: The context window must accommodate all input tokens (10 papers × 8,000 = 80,000) plus the output tokens (3,000) = 83,000 total. Both input and output consume context window space simultaneously.

distractors.A: 8,000 tokens only fits one paper. The requirement is to process all 10 papers simultaneously for cross-paper synthesis.
distractors.B: 16,000 tokens cannot fit even 3 papers. The full input alone requires 80,000 tokens.
distractors.C: Output tokens consume context window space alongside input. The model must maintain the full context while generating output.

questions.stem: An ML model is required as a prerequisite before creating a vector database. What role does this model play in the database creation process?

options.text: It manages the database's auto-scaling and load balancing
It processes input data into dense vector embeddings that are stored in the database
It generates the database schema and table definitions
It validates data quality before insertion into the database

explanation.correct: A vector database is filled with dense vectors produced by processing input data through an embedding model. The ML model converts raw data (text, images) into numerical vector representations that capture semantic meaning.

distractors.A: Auto-scaling and load balancing are infrastructure concerns handled by the database service itself, not the embedding model.
distractors.C: Vector databases don't use traditional schemas. The embedding model's role is to produce vectors, not define database structure.
distractors.D: The embedding model transforms data into vectors. Data quality validation is a separate upstream concern.

questions.scenario: A team runs their application on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. They want to add AI-powered semantic search without introducing additional database services or migrating data.
questions.stem: How can they add vector search capabilities to their existing database?

options.text: Store embeddings as JSONB arrays and write custom distance functions in PL/pgSQL
Enable the pgvector extension to add native vector data types and optimized similarity search operators
Export data to OpenSearch nightly and query both systems in parallel
Use PostgreSQL's built-in full-text search with tsvector as a substitute for vector embeddings

explanation.correct: The pgvector extension for Amazon RDS PostgreSQL provides native vector data types, indexing (IVFFlat, HNSW), and similarity search operators. It adds vector capabilities directly within the existing database without additional services.

distractors.A: JSONB arrays lack optimized vector indexing and distance calculations. Custom functions would be orders of magnitude slower than pgvector's native operations.
distractors.C: Dual-database architectures add complexity and data synchronization challenges. pgvector keeps everything in one database.
distractors.D: tsvector is for keyword-based full-text search. It cannot perform semantic similarity search on dense vector embeddings.

questions.scenario: A financial services firm is deciding between RAG and fine-tuning to customize their foundation model for regulatory compliance questions.
questions.stem: In which situations would fine-tuning be preferred OVER RAG? (Select TWO)

options.text: When the model needs to consistently adopt a specific response style, tone, or structured output format
When the customization requires the model to internalize domain reasoning patterns that prompting cannot reliably produce
When compliance regulations change quarterly and the model needs to reflect current rules
When the primary need is accessing up-to-date external documents at query time
When compute budget is zero and no GPU resources are available

explanation.correct: Fine-tuning is preferred for persistent behavioral changes — adopting specific styles/formats and internalizing reasoning patterns. These become part of the model's weights, producing consistent behavior without requiring prompt engineering on every call.

distractors.C: Quarterly regulatory changes are best served by RAG (update knowledge base) rather than retraining quarterly.
distractors.D: Accessing current external documents at query time is exactly RAG's strength — it retrieves without retraining.
distractors.E: Fine-tuning requires GPU compute. Zero budget makes RAG or in-context learning the only viable options.

questions.scenario: A data science team creates a model selection rubric. They identify criteria that determine whether a model can physically run in their environment vs criteria that determine whether it performs well on their task.
questions.stem: Which criteria determine whether a model CAN run in the target environment (feasibility), vs how well it performs (quality)? Select the TWO that are feasibility constraints.

options.text: Available GPU memory and compute capacity to serve the model
Context window size relative to the application's input/output requirements
F1 score on a held-out evaluation dataset
BLEU score on translation benchmarks
User satisfaction ratings from beta testing

explanation.correct: GPU capacity and context window size are hard feasibility constraints — if the model can't fit in memory or can't process the required input length, it simply cannot function. These must be satisfied before quality metrics matter.

distractors.C: F1 score measures quality/performance on a task. A model can run (feasibility) but perform poorly (quality).
distractors.D: BLEU score measures translation quality. It indicates performance level, not whether the model can physically run.
distractors.E: Satisfaction ratings measure quality from the user perspective. They don't determine whether the model can technically operate.

questions.scenario: A company builds a product quality inspection system using camera images from the assembly line, audio from machine vibrations, and text from maintenance logs.
questions.stem: Why might an ensemble of specialized models outperform a single multi-modal model for this system? (Select TWO)

options.text: Each modality has specific embedding representations that specialized models can optimize for independently
Combining multiple specialized models can achieve better overall performance than any single model across all modalities
Ensemble models always have lower latency than single models
Specialized models require no training data for their respective modalities
Ensembles eliminate the need for data preprocessing on any modality

explanation.correct: Each modality (image, audio, text) has distinct embedding structures that specialized models handle optimally. Ensemble methods combine these specialized strengths, often exceeding any single model's multi-modal performance.

distractors.C: Ensembles typically increase latency because multiple models must process input. The benefit is accuracy, not speed.
distractors.D: All models require training data. Specialized models need modality-specific data — images for vision models, audio for acoustic models.
distractors.E: Each modality still requires appropriate preprocessing (image resizing, audio spectrogram conversion, text tokenization). Ensembles don't eliminate this need.

questions.scenario: A company stores thousands of internal documents across multiple S3 buckets. They want their Bedrock FM to answer employee questions using this internal knowledge without requiring custom embedding pipelines or vector database management.
questions.stem: Which service provides this end-to-end managed capability?

options.text: AWS Glue with custom ETL jobs transforming documents into searchable formats
Amazon Kendra enterprise search with manual FAQ configuration
Amazon Comprehend for document classification and entity extraction
Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock — handling embedding, vector storage, and retrieval automatically

explanation.correct: Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock provides fully managed RAG — automatically handling document chunking, embedding generation, vector storage, and retrieval to connect the FM to company data without custom pipeline code.

distractors.A: Glue handles ETL but doesn't provide embedding generation, vector storage, or FM integration for RAG.
distractors.B: Kendra provides search but is a separate service from Bedrock's integrated knowledge base. The question asks about Bedrock FM integration without custom pipelines.
distractors.C: Comprehend extracts entities and classifies documents but does not provide RAG, vector storage, or FM-integrated retrieval.

questions.scenario: A company's FM handles customer queries well for general topics but consistently produces the wrong output format — returning prose paragraphs instead of the structured JSON their API expects. Few-shot examples in prompts work 80% of the time but fail for complex edge cases.
questions.stem: Which customization approach should they escalate to?

options.text: RAG with a knowledge base of correctly formatted JSON examples
Pre-training a new model from scratch with JSON-formatted training data
Fine-tuning with labeled examples of the correct input-output format to permanently modify the model's behavior
Increasing the model's temperature to explore more diverse output formats

explanation.correct: Fine-tuning is appropriate when in-context learning (prompting) cannot reliably produce the desired behavior. It permanently modifies model weights to consistently output the target format, addressing the 20% failure rate on edge cases.

distractors.A: RAG retrieves information but doesn't reliably change output format behavior. The model already understands JSON — it just doesn't consistently produce it.
distractors.B: Pre-training from scratch is massively expensive and unnecessary. The model works well on content — only the format behavior needs correction.
distractors.D: Higher temperature increases randomness and would make format consistency worse, not better.
